UHF transmitter on B-52 disrupted while object paced it and resumed when it left.

The B-52 was 'unexpectedly diverted' by an unidentified general officer to overfly the UFO.

Evidence_Records.description: Wing history states Echo shutdown at 0845 on 16 Mar 1967: all 10 LFs lost strategic alert nearly simultaneously; 'normal controlled shutdown'; faults VRSA ch.9 (G&C No-Go) and ch.12 (Logic Coupler No-Go).

Wing history says UFO rumors for Echo were 'disproven' and a Mobile Strike Team checking November Flight LFs reported nothing unusual — conflicts with testimony that crews saw UFOs near Echo LFs; interview sourcing of that statement undocumented.

Kingston George (SI 1993): film debrief and secrecy cautions occurred; film later destroyed; supports existence of a classified filming and of a debrief, differs on interpretation and date (22 Sep).

Launch lists show Atlas D 245D ABRES LORV-3 RV test on 15 Sep 1964 15:27 UTC (08:27 PDT) as a PARTIAL FAILURE (manual cutoff after SECO); book cites 'Atlas D 245H'. A launch malfunction is an untested alternative explanation for a warhead falling short.

Column notes three Atlas silos were destroyed by fuel explosions at Walker, a stressful context. Hastings dates the column June 2001; copy index says Oct 2001 — date unresolved.

Hartmann, Wertheimer, Levine); report 965 pp paperback/1,485 hardcover; also notes consultant Rothberg 'about 100 cases, three or four puzzling' and critics that enigmatic cases were 'buried'. Book's '91 sightings' and 'nearly 30%' not confirmed here.

Frazier: Wikipedia says he worked full-time at Sandia 1983-2006 writing about its research and editing the Sandia Lab News for the last 11 years; consistent with book's 'two decades'; Wikipedia biography itself discloses Sandia, though the SI masthead may not.
Hastings' Ch13 argues the identity/affiliation of skeptics undermines their conclusions (genetic/ad hominem reasoning). It contains no new incident evidence; its value is argumentative.

Werlich's Memo for the Record (24 Oct 1968), quoted by Shough: 'Initially the target traveled approximately 2½ mile in 3 sec or at about 3,000 mi/hr' (arithmetic: 2.5 mi/3 s = 3,000 mph). His 29 Oct telex instead says an echo closed from 3 mi to ~1 mi off the left wing, with no speed. The Blue Book file therefore has TWO different official speed statements; neither is '2 miles in 3 s = 3,900 mph'.
Evidence_Records.provenance: SRC023 (quoting Blue Book file); verification of original memo pending

Evidence_Records.description: Origin of '3,900': Shough reconstructs it as the simple average of two rates computed from echo displacements relative to the B-52 between frames 771-772 and 772-773, using antenna paint-time-corrected intervals (3.8 s and 1.3 s): ~1,990 kt and ~5,870 kt, co-altitude upper limits, mean ~3,900 KNOTS (~4,450 statute mph). Hence Clark's number is knots, a mean of very unequal rates, an upper limit, and not '2 miles per sweep'.

Analyst recomputation (this project): from Shough's measured echo positions (771: 138 deg/1.62 NM; 772: 242 deg/1.05 NM; 773: 40 deg/1.05 NM; azimuth from nose, slant range) the displacements are 2.13 and 2.06 NM. With a naive 3.0 s per frame: ~2,560 and ~2,470 kt (~2,950/2,850 mph) relative speed. With Shough's paint-time intervals (3.8, 1.3 s): ~2,020 kt and ~5,710 kt (matches Shough ~1,990/5,870 within ~3%); their simple mean is ~3,865 kt (reproducing '3,900'), but the time-weighted mean over the 5.1 s is only ~2,960 kt (~3,400 mph). Script: database/build/analysis/minot_speed.py.
Evidence_Records.provenance: Derived from SRC023 numerical values; not independent measurement of the photographs

Evidence_Records.description: Assumptions behind any speed figure: (i) the three echoes are one target (Shough: cannot be justified from two possibly unrelated echoes; elongated echoes are suggestive but not conclusive); (ii) co-altitude (a depression angle lowers true separation; e.g. at 50 deg the naive horizontal speed would be ~1,650 kt, ~1,900 mph); (iii) range scale inferred (~5 NM display, no indicator on photographs); (iv) only 14 of probably >100 frames survive. The result is an upper-limit estimate, not a measurement of a 3,900 mph object.

[SUPERSEDED by EVD034] Timeline dispute between analysts: Shough concludes frames 771-783 were taken late in the event near the missed approach (so the 'fast' echo transit is not the start); Poher concludes the radarscope clock (0906Z) runs ~9 min ahead of the approach-controller clock so frames coincide with radio loss at ~0858 COM when the B-52 was ~21 nm out (early). The question of when the high-speed transit occurred relative to ground sightings is unresolved in the sources I read.

[PARTLY SUPERSEDED by EVD040] Dispatcher log vs B-52 explanation: entries 0828-0830Z mention jet engines; the B-52 low approach/missed approach was ~0904-0917 COM (Poher). So the Blue Book statement that 'later sightings ... correlate with' the B-52 low approach is plausible for entries after ~0900Z but not demonstrated for the 0800-0858Z entries; and entries 0940-1010Z (after the log says the B-52 landed at 0940Z) describe a stationary object west of N-7 on/near the ground, which the B-52 cannot explain.

Analyst astronomical check (this project; simple GMST/precession, Minot AFB 48.42N 101.36W, 24 Oct 1968): Sirius altitude 11-23 deg, azimuth 132-162 deg (SE to SSE) from 0800Z to 1010Z; Vega 7 deg->-2 deg altitude, azimuth 325-348 deg (NW-NNW), setting ~0940Z. Dispatcher entries 0800Z 'S/E of N-7' fit Sirius direction; entries 0940-1010Z 'west of N-7' do not (~110 deg off); Blue Book cites Vega at azimuth 345 at 0435 local (matches my 342 deg) but the pilot's light was 'west-northwest' (~50 deg away) - requires check of the AF Forms 117. Script: database/build/analysis/minot_sirius.py.
Evidence_Records.provenance: Computed; positions accurate to ~0.5 deg; atmospheric refraction ignored

Evidence_Records.description: Blue Book's own text (SRC025) says no data were submitted for the possible 0335 local air visual and 0352 weather-radar paint, and that the pilot's Form 117 puts his sighting at ~0435 local, not 0335: official file acknowledges data gaps in the timeline; Hastings' narrative does not.

Transcript time base: COM clock is Zulu (landing 0940Z matches dispatcher log and pilot's request to 'touch down at 40 past'; CDT = Z-5 with DST still in effect on 24 Oct 1968). All earlier 'local time' mismatches in the file are 1-hr/20-min inconsistencies in individual witness entries, not in the transcript.

Transcript 0852: controller says weather radar also sees the object at the B-52's 1:00, 3 miles; B-52 replies 'We have nothing on our airborne radar and I'm in some pretty thick haze'. Omitted from the book's narrative, which says RAPCON was told weather radar tracked the object 'near Bowbells, ND, 38 nm NW' (Bowbells does not appear in the transcript).

Pilot radio reports (transcript 0902/0904): echo at ~1.25-1.5 mi left of the aircraft from 'about the time we left 200 to about 14 [thousand]' and 'till about 10'; radio trouble began 'exactly' then. Together with the ~10-11.5 k ft altitude derived from the photos, this places frames 771-783 in the latter part of the echo episode (about 0858-0902Z), 3-5 min after first report near FL200.

CORRECTION to EVD027: the Shough/Poher 'early vs late' contrast is narrower than I first reported. Both altitude models put the frames at ~10-11.5 k ft MSL, i.e., late in the echo episode and after the FL200 turn; they differ mainly on clock offset (Shough 7-8 min with caveats; Poher 9 min; my linear-descent estimate 5-6 min). The fast transit in frames 771-773 is therefore not the 'initial' fast approach described by Werlich/McCaslin. See documents/minot_1968_timeline.md.

Partin's Form 117 (30 Oct 1968) describes a stationary 'bright orange ball of light' ~15 mi away at 1 o'clock on/just above the ground, 'miniature sun placed on the ground'; it does not mention an oblong shape, windows, or a tubular section. Those details appear in later interviews quoted by the book (Partin: 'oblong ... windows'; Runyon: barn-sized with a tube, 32 yrs later). The form's sketch shows a small circle with 'a very dim ring of soft white light'.

Partin's reported time (0430-0435 CDT = 0930-0935Z) does not match the transcript (downwind leg 0910Z = 0410 CDT; final 0928Z); the file's annotation 'should be 0335 CDT' (an hour earlier) matches neither. Blue Book used 0435 for its Vega calculation.

Vega test of the Blue Book 'air visual' explanation (analyst calculation): bearing OK — Partin's 1 o'clock from heading 290 magnetic is ~328-332 deg true (declination 8-12 E) vs Vega az 336-337 deg at 0906-0910Z. Brightness FAILS — Vega was only ~1.4 deg->0.4 deg high (airmass 23-33): extinction ~4.6-6.9 mag at 0906Z (k 0.2-0.3), so Vega would appear ~mag 5-7 or fainter, not a 'bright orange ball'/'miniature sun'. Also the light 'remained stationary as we flew toward it' and the aircraft passed ~1 mi south of it, which a star cannot do. A terrestrial light (e.g., ground light, other aircraft) or misjudged range is more consistent than Vega.
Evidence_Records.provenance: Computed; positions ~0.5 deg; extinction coefficients assumed

Evidence_Records.description: Ground-observer forms: Smith — reddish burnt orange, twinkling like a star, slight green, on the horizon, ~15 deg elevation, no edges (compass mark appears S-SW; Sirius was SE-SSE: low-res reading, needs checking); O'Connor — white ball -> dim green -> dim amber, facing south, final mark ESE-SE at ~20 deg (matches Sirius direction/elevation) and a Blue Book annotation 'Characteristic colors of Sirius'; Isley — lights 'like head lights or landing lights' on the front and a green flashing light toward the middle or rear, shape/size not determinable, two objects at one time (more aircraft-like); Bond — point of light with fuzzy edges ~10 mi from N-7, two objects, second seen ~3 min, Mohall town lights 4 mi. The observers' descriptions are not uniform: some fit a scintillating Sirius, one suggests an aircraft.

Internal conflict in the file: transcript 0913Z says missile-site personnel 'don't see anything anymore'; dispatcher entries 0940-1010Z say N-7 still sees an object 3 mi west, stationary near the ground. Different sites/time bases are not established.

CORRECTION to EVD028: the transcript shows the B-52 was in the Minot area around 0828-0834Z ('TA calibration check to rw 11', climbing out on heading 290 at 0834), so the 0828-0830Z 'jet engines heard' entries may well be the B-52 — partly supporting the Blue Book aircraft explanation for the earliest entries. The post-0940Z entries (object W of N-7 after the B-52 landed) remain unexplained by it.

Origin of the 3,000 mph figure: FTD Memo for the Record 24 Oct 1968 (doc 5) records Lt Col Werlich's telephone account: 'At about 0300 hours local, a B-52 ... 39 miles northwest of Minot ... sighted an unidentified blip on their radar. Initially the target traveled approximately 2½ mile in 3 sec or at about 3,000 mi/hr.' The memo also says 14 other people in separate locations reported a similar object, and that Werlich did not yet know whether ground observers had looked at stellar bodies. The speed is therefore a verbal, same-day estimate relayed second-hand. Note the stated time (~0300 local) is ~1 h earlier than the transcript's radar/radio events (~0358 local).

Werlich's own assessment (doc 12, phone 31 Oct 1968): 'Most of the original sightings were of the aircraft'; 'Almost 80 per cent were looking at the B-52'; the B-52 radar event and visual 'correlated pretty well'; the one he could not identify is the radar/aircraft event; the air-visual location (TACAN 320 radial, 16 NM) is farm fields with 'nothing there that would produce this type of light'; base lights are visible 50 miles away; the crew could receive but not transmit and used IDENT squawks; 'it couldn't be a malfunction because they transmitted before and afterwards'; scope photos were not taken at first, 'until the pilot said why don't you take some photos. This was towards the end.' The book presents Werlich's data but not his opinion that most ground sightings were the B-52.

Oscar-7 intrusion (doc 12): Werlich says the padlock/combination door had been opened; three similar occurrences in the previous 2-3 years were all traced to Air Police who had been in the service on those areas; '99 chances out of 100' it was someone with a key; a lieutenant found no car/tire/footprint evidence next day; local authorities investigating; Werlich planned to survey with a Geiger counter. The book does not mention the intrusion or the prior look-alike cases.

Pressure to play down: FTD memo 30 Oct 1968 (doc 10) — Col Pullen (HQ SAC) asked Quintanilla for a preliminary report 'so that he could give it to General Stewart to get this thing simmered down' and to 'hit a little heavy on what has happened to other aircraft on occasions like this, this would help play the issue down.' Quintanilla also tells Pullen he suspects an internal radar malfunction or inversion-caused anomalous blip and celestial scintillation, sent nobody (staff of four), and had not yet received times. TWX 1 Nov (doc 25) calls the case 'fairly routine' and 'most probably a plasma of the ball-lightning class' before raw data arrived; SAC TWX 7 Nov (doc 26) says the SAC commander and staff were 'extremely interested.' Supports the book's theme that the Air Force evaluation was hasty and shaped by command interest, though the Blue Book memos also show attempts to get data (doc 11).

Doc 15 (Werlich's list of ground observers; 0308-0325 local) repeats that SSgt Smith at Oscar-1 'saw the object separate in two parts and go in opposite directions and return and pass under each other,' with a handwritten Blue Book comment: 'Smith does not say this on 117.' My reading of Smith's AF 117 agrees (reddish burnt orange light 'as a star might twinkle,' no separation). The book (12835-12840) relays the separation detail from the Wing Security Controller's summary via Tulien without this caveat. Isley, Adams and Jablonski forms do mention two objects approaching and one disappearing.

Weather-radar evidence: the transcript (0852) says the weather radar also saw the object, but Blue Book staff phoned Minot on 8 and 13 Nov 1968 specifically to ask about the weather radar and could not reach Werlich (docs 27, 29). No weather-radar record or description appears in the case-file documents I read; the book's 'Bowbells, 38 nm NW' detail is not in them.

Project 10073 record (doc 3): observation 24/0030-0530Z (4 h 48 min); photos: No; conclusions — ground visual 'Probable (AIRCRAFT) (B-52)' and 'Probable Astro (SIRIUS)'; radar 'Possible (PLASMA)'; air-visual 'Possible (PLASMA)'. The official record is therefore a mixed aircraft/star/plasma attribution, not a single cause.

Independent measurement (analyst, scans at 300 ppi): ring peaks in frame 771 at 60/134/208 px (74 px = 0.5 NM, i.e. 148 px/NM) and hole edge 266 px = 2.14 NM with Shough's offset — matching Shough's 2.1 NM. Strongest local blobs: frame 772 at 1.09 NM (Shough 1.05), screen angle 124 deg; frame 773 at 1.08 NM (Shough 1.05), 282 deg. Angular separation 158 deg equals Shough's. Displacement 2.14 NM (Shough 2.06, +4%).

Sensitivity to range-scale calibration: with Shough's offset (rings at 0.75/1.25/1.75 NM) the 772->773 displacement is 2.14 NM = ~2,565 kt at 3.0 s or ~5,920 kt at 1.3 s; if instead range is linear from the centre (rings at 0.5/1.0/1.5 NM) the displacement is 1.46 NM = ~1,750 kt at 3.0 s or ~4,040 kt at 1.3 s. The unexplained calibration (no scale indicator on the photos) therefore shifts speeds by ~30%.

Frame 771 (half-swept): the reported echo at 1.62 NM lies on/inside the third range ring; azimuthal ring-brightness profile shows only small variations (peak 135-140 vs ring ~80-95 at 4-20 deg screen angle) that I cannot separate from ring noise. I could NOT independently confirm that echo. The 771->772 displacement (and the '1,990 kt' rate) therefore rests on Shough's identification.

AF Forms 117 of Adams and Jablonski (viewed at low resolution): Adams — head lights/lights at an air facility; lights reddish orange changing to white and green, self-luminous, very bright, size/shape hard to distinguish; annotation 'see characteristic colors of Sirius'; en route to N-7 another object appeared; they came close then one disappeared; compass A at ~SE. Jablonski — two objects dispatched to N-7; one at the same speed moving toward the other, one vanished; glowing orange-red, white, greenish; 'rather solid', 'very wide and slender', edges fuzzy, 'much brighter than a star'; annotation 'Sirius has m of -1.6'. Combined with Isley and Bond: the maintenance/security observers describe two lights converging with one disappearing — compatible with Sirius plus the B-52, or a pair of aircraft, but not established.

The 90th SMW's own report to FTD (SRC032) counts 148 objects reported by 143 personnel over three nights (31 Jul 75/70; 1 Aug 29/27; 2 Aug 44/46) — about one 'object' per observer — and describes them as mostly round, pinhead-to-nickel sized with colored lights flashing every 1-2 seconds, in V/echelon/cross/box formations, silent. The book, which relies on the Anspaugh log, does not mention this report, its counts, or these descriptors (checked by text search). Analyst note: scintillation-like flashing, star-like angular sizes and the mass-reporting pattern are what one expects from stars/planets under an inversion; they do not rule out something else.

Blue Book addendum of 20 Sep 1965 (SRC033): contemporaneous binocular and 40x-theodolite observations (Sioux Army Depot guard; nine military observers; Geodetic Survey Team) describe star-sized or pinhead-sized objects, some moving, and on four occasions 'a roaring jet-like noise at some distance behind' — contradicting the 6 Aug report's 'no sound' and suggesting aircraft in at least some cases. The theodolite observation (object in the Big Dipper resolving to three white objects) is an instrumented one rarely seen in such cases. Book does not mention these.

A skeptical reviewer's reading of the Blue Book file (SRC034): reports were short, lacked positional data, clustered ~0500Z (2300 MDT), and plausibly involve Jupiter, Capella, Saturn, Vega, Altair, Betelgeuse, Echo 2 and aircraft under an inversion; Blue Book never assigned specific explanations to individual Warren reports; a Blue Book sergeant (Moody) asked for positional data and was ignored. This supports BOTH sides in part: the 'stars' label was weakly supported (Blue Book gave no case-by-case identification) yet the file also lacks any positional data to prove anything else.

Analyst sky test (PyEphem 4.2.1; Cheyenne 41.15N 104.82W; script warren_sky_1965.py), 1 Aug 1965. If the Anspaugh log times are Mountain (Warren local): Jupiter (mag -1.9) rose ~0300 and stood at alt 9-13 deg, az 68-71 deg at 0317-0340; Aldebaran alt 15-19 deg az 81-85; Capella alt 26-29 az 50-53; Saturn alt ~41 az 175-182; Vega alt 37-41 az 290-292; Deneb alt 61-65. The 0340 entry 'one UFO at 70 deg azimuth' matches Jupiter's azimuth (71 deg); 'seven/six UFOs east' (0320-0325) and 'five going east' (Sioux Depot 0335) lie in the direction of Jupiter/Aldebaran/Capella; at 0400 'four NW, three NE' fits Vega/Deneb (WNW) and Capella/Jupiter (NE). But entries at 0130-0250 MDT have only Saturn, Capella (low NE), Vega, Altair, Deneb, Fomalhaut — no Jupiter. If the log times are Eastern (WPAFB; 2 h earlier locally) every entry falls before Jupiter rose and the match fails (Jupiter and Aldebaran not yet above the horizon). The time zone of the log is not stated in the book; Printy's '~0500Z' cluster (2300 MDT = 0100 EDT) fits the Eastern reading for the first entries. The test is therefore suggestive for some entries under one assumption, inconclusive overall.

Log internal timing: the Anspaugh entries mix call times and event times (e.g., 4:05 call about a 4:00 report; 4:40 call about 3:00 and 3:17 reports; later entries 3:20-3:40 follow the 4:40 call). Entries are not in chronological order and carry no time zone, so whether they are Eastern (Blue Book) or Mountain (Warren) cannot be determined from the text I have. The original memorandum and Hynek's printing (UFO Experience, 1972) were not examined.

Bolender document: the key sentence is verbatim in NICAP's transcription ('reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and are not part of the Blue Book system (Atch 10)'). Differences from the book: NICAP calls it a draft, not a memorandum; whether it was signed or sent to all commands is not shown; the 16 attachments are missing; the same document says there is no evidence Blue Book reports served any intelligence function. The sentence supports 'national-security reports are outside Blue Book' but does not show that nuclear-site UFO reports existed in those channels.

Ch.16 states Blue Book 'blithely dismissed the sighting reports at each base as having no merit.' For Minot the file shows otherwise: Blue Book assigned aircraft/Sirius/plasma attributions, labelled the radar and air-visual 'possible plasma', and the file records SAC pressure to play the issue down (EVD044) — so the process was influenced, but the stated conclusions were specific explanations, not blanket dismissal. For Warren, Blue Book's disposition was 'insufficient data'/stars/'inversion effect' with no case-by-case identification (EVD054).
